title: "Preface"

::: {.data-provided-by}
**Data provided by:** Matt Wachowiak, Shawn Burton · *University of Utah*
:::

This is a guided tour through an analysis of how the mouse olfactory bulb
represents odor concentration. The data are paired glomerular
calcium-imaging responses recorded by the Wachowiak lab at the University
of Utah: ~400 imaged glomeruli concatenated across four mice, exposed to
the same 59 odorants at two concentrations [@burton2022olfactory]. The
basic question is: **how does the high-concentration glomerular pattern
relate to the low-concentration one?** Per-glomerulus amplification?
Group-level remixing? Something less structured? etc.

The punchline is that the remapping is a **structured, low-rank,
cluster-aligned linear map**. A partial-least-squares regression with eight
latent components captures most of the predictable held-out variance; the
remaining nonlinear structure is small enough that a 20-model horse race
— covering kernel methods, tree ensembles, neural nets, and local methods
— finds no method that substantially beats the linear ceiling. The
coefficient matrix `B` is organized by NMF receptor-class clusters: about
40% of `B`'s predictive energy lives in within-cluster blocks (≈ 50σ above
a cluster-label permutation null), and the cluster-block structure
reproduces across all five preprocessing variants we tested and across a
completely different estimator (full-rank ridge regression). In a
nutshell, concentration coding, in the bulb, obeys group-specific rules,
and the groups are defined by their similar tuning.

## How this book is organized

[**The Analysis**](main.ipynb) — the main story, in five sections plus an
appendix. §1 establishes that a linear rule exists. §2 places `B`
between two domain-specific nulls (multiplicative gain vs. random
retuning). §3 introduces the cluster-block decomposition and shows
that `B`'s structure is organized by NMF clusters. §4 confirms the
clusters are anatomically real on the dorsal OB. §5 pulls the three
claims into a synthesis. The appendix carries the LV1 outer-product
loadings, a model-zoo comparison, and a methods footnote section.

[**The Model Zoo**](model-zoo.ipynb) — the full horse race that the appendix
summarizes. Twenty regression methods, family-stratified 4-fold CV, same
preprocessing as the canonical pipeline. RidgeCV wins; no nonlinear method
notably beats it. The chapter is a sibling artifact to the main analysis,
useful for confirming that the linear-rule claim isn't an artifact of
choosing PLS-R specifically.

[**References**](references.qmd) — the canonical sources cited throughout.

## Reading notes

The figures are interactive Plotly objects. Hover for hover-text; click on
legend entries to toggle traces; double-click to isolate a single trace.
The chapters render the same notebooks (`notebooks/CONSOLIDATED.ipynb`
and `notebooks/03_model_zoo.ipynb`) that the analysis was developed in,
so any figure you see in the rendered book is reproducible by running
those notebooks against the canonical results in `results/baseline/`.

Code cells in each chapter are *shown* by default but collapsible via the
`</> Code` button in the top-right of each page. Section anchors are
linkable.

## Acknowledgments {.unnumbered}

The data and the framing of the problem come from Matt Wachowiak and Shawn
Burton at the University of Utah. The two nulls the analysis is anchored
on — multiplicative gain and random retuning — are theirs. The
chemometrics machinery (PLS-R, component-selection criteria, permutation
nulls) draws on the Krishnan et al. tutorial [@krishnan2011partial] and the
Van der Voet randomization test [@vandervoet1994comparing]. The Okabe-Ito
palette used in the topographic figures is by Okabe & Ito (2008).

The original messy notebooks live in `~/code/castro-lab-codebase`; this
analysis is the clean rewrite in `~/code/pls-explorer`, sibling to the
broader `~/code/glom-explorer` package.
